takeaways.q: What is the persistent case facts block?
takeaways.a: Transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers) extracted into a structured block included in every prompt, outside summarised history — so summarisation can't destroy them.

takeaways.q: Why does progressive summarisation fail for customer support?
takeaways.a: It systematically destroys the most critical info: numbers, dates, percentages, customer-stated expectations.

takeaways.q: How do you address 'lost in the middle' in aggregated inputs?
takeaways.a: Put a key-findings summary at the beginning and organise details under explicit section headers. Structural fix, not a prompt reminder.

takeaways.q: Why trim tool results before they enter history?
takeaways.a: A 40+ field result is re-sent every turn as history grows. Trim to relevant fields first.

takeaways.q: Why can't you selectively truncate conversation history?
takeaways.a: The API is stateless — each request needs the complete history for coherence. Use case-facts blocks and summarisation instead.

takeaways.q: Upstream fix for context waste in multi-agent systems?
takeaways.a: Make upstream agents return structured data (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of verbose reasoning and raw content.

takeaways.q: Role of prompt caching?
takeaways.a: Mark a stable prefix with a cache_control breakpoint; subsequent requests pay a fraction for cached tokens instead of reprocessing.

traps.trap: Thinking progressive summarisation is safe for transactional data
traps.why: Summarisation destroys numbers, dates, and identifiers. Keep them in a persistent case facts block outside summarised history.

traps.trap: Assuming the 'lost in the middle' effect is solved by telling the model to pay attention to everything
traps.why: The fix is structural: key findings first, explicit section headers. Prompt reminders are unreliable for position effects.

traps.trap: Keeping full tool results in context because 'the model might need them later'
traps.why: Untrimmed 40+ field results exhaust the budget across turns. Trim before they enter history.

traps.trap: Believing conversation history can be selectively truncated without consequences
traps.why: The API is stateless; truncation breaks coherence. Use case facts blocks and summarisation instead.

takeaways.q: Three valid escalation triggers?
takeaways.a: Explicit request for a human (honour immediately); policy exceptions/gaps (not violations); inability to make meaningful progress after a genuine attempt.

takeaways.q: Why is sentiment-based escalation unreliable?
takeaways.a: Frustration doesn't correlate with complexity. Furious + simple issue = resolvable; calm + policy gap = escalate.

takeaways.q: Why is self-reported confidence a poor escalation signal?
takeaways.a: It's poorly calibrated — confidently wrong on hard cases, needlessly unsure on easy ones. (A separate classifier score can be a valid trigger.)

takeaways.q: Frustrated customer, straightforward issue — what do you do?
takeaways.a: Acknowledge the frustration and offer the resolution. Escalate only if they then explicitly ask for a human.

takeaways.q: Customer explicitly asks for a human?
takeaways.a: Escalate immediately — no investigation, no 'let me try first'. Absolute rule.

takeaways.q: Name search returns multiple customer records?
takeaways.a: Ask for disambiguating identifiers (email, phone, order number). Never pick by heuristic like most recent/most active.

takeaways.q: Proportionate first fix for poor escalation calibration?
takeaways.a: Add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples to the system prompt — before any architectural change.

takeaways.q: Policy violation vs policy gap?
takeaways.a: Violation: policy has an answer (outside return window = no). Gap: policy is silent → needs human judgement → escalate.

traps.trap: Sentiment-based escalation seems reasonable but is fundamentally unreliable
traps.why: Frustration ≠ complexity. Furious + simple late delivery is easy; calm + policy gap needs escalation.

traps.trap: Self-reported confidence scores provide a reliable escalation signal
traps.why: LLM self-confidence is poorly calibrated — exactly the failure mode the exam tests.

traps.trap: Attempting to resolve before honouring an explicit human request
traps.why: 'I want a human' → escalate immediately. Absolute rule.

traps.trap: Selecting from ambiguous customer matches using the most recent or most active record
traps.why: Risks privacy violations and wrong actions. Ask for additional identifiers.

takeaways.q: Four elements of structured error context from a failed subagent?
takeaways.a: Failure type (transient/validation/business/permission), what was attempted (query, params, target), partial results gathered, potential alternative approaches.

takeaways.q: Why is silent suppression the worst anti-pattern?
takeaways.a: Empty results marked success → coordinator thinks it searched and found nothing → no retry or alternatives, invisible gaps in output.

takeaways.q: Workflow termination vs intelligent recovery?
takeaways.a: Termination kills the pipeline on one failure, discarding others' good results. Recovery uses structured error context to retry, try alternatives, or proceed with partial results.

takeaways.q: Access failure vs valid empty result?
takeaways.a: Access failure: couldn't reach the source (timeout, permission) → may retry. Valid empty: query ran, no matches → that IS the answer; don't retry.

takeaways.q: When should a subagent propagate an error?
takeaways.a: Only after local recovery for transient failures (retry, fallback, degraded response) fails — include what was attempted and partial results.

takeaways.q: What are coverage annotations for?
takeaways.a: Marking which areas are well-supported vs have gaps from unavailable sources, instead of silently omitting topics.

takeaways.q: What does the coordinator do with structured error context?
takeaways.a: Assess failure type and partial results, then retry with modified params, try an alternative, proceed with partial results, or escalate.

traps.trap: Catching a timeout and returning empty results marked as successful
traps.why: Silent suppression blocks all recovery — the coordinator never tries alternatives. Worst anti-pattern.

traps.trap: Terminating the entire research pipeline when one subagent times out
traps.why: Wastes successful subagents' partial results. Assess and recover in a targeted way.

traps.trap: Returning a generic 'search unavailable' status after retry exhaustion
traps.why: Hides the query, partial results and alternatives. Structured error context enables informed recovery.

traps.trap: Retrying a valid empty result because it looks like a failure
traps.why: The query succeeded with no matches — that is the answer. Retrying always returns nothing.

takeaways.q: What is context degradation and why doesn't a bigger window fix it?
takeaways.a: As verbose output accumulates, the model loses grip on specific findings and talks about 'typical patterns' instead of the actual classes/methods it found. Attention quality, not token limit.

takeaways.q: Primary mitigation for context degradation in exploration?
takeaways.a: Scratchpad files that persist key findings outside the conversation.

takeaways.q: Main benefit of subagent delegation for exploration (beyond parallelism)?
takeaways.a: Context isolation — subagents absorb verbose exploration; the main agent's context stays clean for coordination.

takeaways.q: What is the cold start problem and its fix?
takeaways.a: Phase 2 subagents redo Phase 1 exploration. Fix: summary injection of Phase 1 findings into Phase 2 prompts.

takeaways.q: When should /compact be used?
takeaways.a: Proactively during extended sessions to maintain quality — not only as a last resort at the limit.

takeaways.q: What goes in a crash-recovery state manifest?
takeaways.a: Session ID, current phase, explored paths, key findings, next steps.

takeaways.q: How does context degradation show up in behaviour?
takeaways.a: Generic references instead of the specific class names, methods, and dependency chains discovered earlier.

traps.trap: Increasing the context window to solve context degradation
traps.why: It's not about running out of tokens; a larger window still fills with verbose output.

traps.trap: Assuming subagent delegation is only about parallelisation
traps.why: The primary benefit for exploration is context isolation.

traps.trap: Restarting a session to fix context degradation without saving state
traps.why: Loses all knowledge. Persist findings in scratchpads/state manifests first, then inject them.

traps.trap: Using /compact only when hitting context limits
traps.why: Use it proactively to maintain context quality.

takeaways.q: Why are aggregate accuracy metrics dangerous for automation decisions?
takeaways.a: 97% overall can hide 40% accuracy on a particular document type — teams over-automate.

takeaways.q: What must you validate before automating extractions?
takeaways.a: Accuracy by document type AND field segment — never aggregate alone.

takeaways.q: Why sample high-confidence extractions?
takeaways.a: They're automated and unreviewed. Only stratified sampling of them detects novel error patterns.

takeaways.q: Raw confidence vs actual accuracy?
takeaways.a: Uncalibrated: 0.90 might mean 94% on dates but 82% on amounts.

takeaways.q: How is confidence calibrated?
takeaways.a: Labelled validation sets with ground truth → compare confidence to actual accuracy → calibration curves per field type per document type.

takeaways.q: How do you allocate limited reviewer capacity?
takeaways.a: Highest-uncertainty items first (low-confidence fields, historically problematic doc types) — not evenly.

takeaways.q: Correct sequence before reducing human review?
takeaways.a: Measure accuracy by segment → calibrate confidence → set calibrated thresholds → stratified sampling → reduce review only on validated segments.

traps.trap: Using aggregate accuracy (e.g., 97%) to justify automating all high-confidence extractions
traps.why: Aggregates hide per-type failures. Validate by document type and field segment.

traps.trap: Only sampling low-confidence extractions for human review
traps.why: Novel errors in automated high-confidence items are only caught by stratified sampling of those items.

traps.trap: Using raw model confidence scores without calibration
traps.why: 0.90 means different accuracy per field. Calibrate on labelled sets.

traps.trap: Spreading reviewer capacity evenly across all extractions
traps.why: Wastes time on high-confidence items. Prioritise the highest-uncertainty items.

takeaways.q: Five components every claim should carry in multi-agent research?
takeaways.a: Claim, source URL, document name, relevant excerpt, publication date.

takeaways.q: Why does attribution fail in synthesis?
takeaways.a: Synthesis agents compress and paraphrase; without explicit instructions to preserve claim–source mappings, attribution dies.

takeaways.q: Two credible sources conflict. What does synthesis do?
takeaways.a: Annotate both values with full attribution and dates; let the consumer decide. Don't pick one.

takeaways.q: Why are publication dates critical?
takeaways.a: Different dates often explain different numbers as a trend, not a contradiction.

takeaways.q: How should synthesis render different content types?
takeaways.a: Financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.

takeaways.q: Where in the pipeline is attribution most often lost?
takeaways.a: At the synthesis step — its prompt must require every claim to be traceable.

takeaways.q: Analysis agent hits conflicting field values?
takeaways.a: Complete the analysis with both values preserved and annotated; the coordinator/consumer resolves.

traps.trap: Selecting the most recent source when two credible sources conflict
traps.why: Picking one destroys information. Annotate both with attribution and dates.

traps.trap: Assuming different numbers from different sources are contradictions
traps.why: Different collection dates often explain them. Require dates in structured outputs.

traps.trap: Allowing the synthesis agent to paraphrase without preserving claim-source mappings
traps.why: Attribution dies in summarisation. Synthesis must preserve and merge mappings.

traps.trap: Rendering all content types in a uniform format (all prose, all tables, or all lists)
traps.why: Tables for financials, prose for news, lists for technical findings.
